title: Financial Literacy · Episode 3
chapters: Super housekeeping: find, combine and check your fund

units.t: Financial Literacy. Episode three.
In this episode: Superannuation explained, Super housekeeping: find, combine and check your fund, Insurance without the confusion and Income protection: insuring your pay.
Part one. Superannuation explained.
It's probably your second-biggest asset after a home, and most people barely look at it.
Ten minutes here could be worth tens of thousands.
What super is.
Superannuation, or super, is money set aside during your working life and invested to support you in retirement.
It became compulsory for most employees in 1992, and Australia's system now holds more than $4 trillion, one of the largest retirement savings pools in the world.
Your employer must pay a percentage of your ordinary earnings into your fund on top of your wages.
This Super Guarantee rose to 12% on 1 July 2025.
On a $70,000 salary, that is $8,400 a year.
Check your payslips and fund account to confirm it is arriving, and report unpaid super to the ATO.
Self-employed people aren't covered, so they make their own contributions.
Why it grows.
Your super isn't sitting in a bank account.
Your fund invests it in a mix of Australian and international shares, property, infrastructure, bonds and cash.
Most people stay in their fund's default 'balanced' or 'growth' option, often a MySuper product.
Because the money stays invested for 40 years or more, compounding does enormous work: much of your final balance comes from investment returns, not from contributions.
Balances will fall in some years when markets drop, but this is a very long game, and the simple idea is small amounts, invested steadily, growing into a large sum.
Because it is locked away until retirement, it is also protected from being spent early.
Fees matter.
Fees are charged as a dollar amount, a percentage of your balance, or both.
A difference of just 0.
5% or 1% a year sounds tiny.
Over a working lifetime, though, it can mean tens of thousands of dollars less in retirement, because fees compound just as returns do.
The ATO's free YourSuper comparison tool lets you compare MySuper products by fees and past returns.
The regulator, APRA, also tests these products each year, and funds that fail the performance test must tell their members.
Compare your fund against others at least occasionally, rather than leaving it untouched for decades.
One fund, with cover.
Many people end up with several super accounts from different jobs, each charging fees and often insurance premiums.
Since 2021, your existing fund is generally 'stapled' to you and follows you to new jobs, which helps.
Link the ATO to your myGov account to find all your accounts, including lost super, and consolidate them online in minutes.
Most funds automatically include life cover, paid to your beneficiaries, total and permanent disability cover and sometimes income protection.
Premiums come out of your balance.
It can be good value, but check the amounts suit you.
Before closing an account, check whether it holds insurance you want, as that cover ends when the account closes.
Nominate your beneficiaries too; a binding nomination gives more certainty.
Tax perks and access.
Super is taxed lightly to encourage saving.

Employer contributions are generally taxed at 15%, below most people's income tax rate, and investment earnings are generally taxed at no more than 15%, though extra tax is planned for very large balances.
You can add extra through salary sacrifice or personal contributions you claim as a tax deduction, up to an annual cap.
Lower-income earners may qualify for government co-contributions.
You can generally access super once you reach preservation age, 60 if born on or after 1 July 1964, and retire, or at 65 even if you keep working.
Early access is allowed only in narrow cases such as severe financial hardship.
Be wary of anyone offering early release; illegal schemes bring heavy penalties.
Check the ATO website for current limits.
The key idea: Super is money set aside from your pay and invested for retirement, and your employer must add to it on top of your wages.
Part two. Super housekeeping: find, combine and check your fund.
Many Australians have super scattered across funds they barely remember, each quietly charging fees.
A once-a-year check-up can tidy it up, but there are traps to look out for before you hit 'combine'.
The scattered super problem.
Picture someone who worked at a café, then a retail chain, then an office.
Before the rules changed, each employer could open a new default super account.
Each one may charge administration and investment fees, and sometimes insurance premiums, nibbling at small balances.
Since late 2021, stapling means your existing fund generally follows you to a new job unless you choose otherwise.
But old accounts don't vanish by themselves.
The quickest way to see them all is myGov, with the ATO linked: it lists every account in your name, plus lost super and unclaimed super held by the ATO.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Check insurance first.
This is the trap that catches people.
Many super accounts include default insurance: cover if you die or become totally and permanently disabled, and sometimes income protection.
When you roll an account into another fund, the old cover normally ends.
If your health has changed since you joined, you may struggle to get equivalent cover elsewhere.
Before consolidating, download the insurance details for each account and compare the type of cover, the amounts and the cost.
Cover in an account that has stopped receiving contributions can also be switched off after a period of inactivity unless you ask to keep it.
Decide deliberately, rather than letting a rollover decide for you.
Keep, or combine.
Defined benefit funds, common in older public sector and some corporate schemes, calculate your benefit by formula rather than balance, so leaving can mean giving up valuable entitlements.
Some employers also pay into a specific fund with cheaper fees or tailored insurance.
Funds can no longer charge exit fees, but investments may be sold and re-bought during a transfer, and your money can be out of the market for a few days.
Once you have chosen a fund, select the accounts and the receiving fund in myGov, and the request is sent electronically.
Transfers take days to weeks.
Check that old accounts show zero, tell your employer which fund to use, and avoid anyone charging to 'find your lost super'.
The official tools are free.
Is your fund any good.
A single account is tidy, but it should also be a good one.
The ATO's YourSuper comparison tool ranks MySuper products, the default options most people are in, by fees and net returns over several years.
Under the annual performance test, products that underperform a benchmark must write to their members to say so, and repeat failures can be closed to new members.
If you get one of those letters, take it seriously.
Compare long-term returns after fees, not one good year, and check that the investment mix suits how long you have until retirement.
Fees that look small as a percentage can add up to a large sum over decades, thanks to the same compounding that grows your balance.
Beneficiaries and check-ups.
Super is generally held in trust, so it does not automatically follow your will.
Most funds let you nominate who receives your balance and any insurance payout if you die.
A valid binding nomination generally directs the trustee to pay the people you name, while a non-binding one is only a guide.
Some binding nominations lapse after a set period unless renewed, and marriage, separation or a new child can make an old nomination wrong.
Set a yearly reminder to check contributions, fees, insurance, investment option and beneficiaries.
Moneysmart.
gov.
au has plain-language guides to every step.
The key idea: Old super accounts keep charging fees, so it pays to find them even though stapling now slows new duplicates.
Part three. Insurance without the confusion.
Most of us pay for insurance for years without reading a word of the policy.
Here's how it actually works, and how to avoid a nasty surprise at claim time.
Pooling and priorities.
Thousands of people each pay a small, predictable premium into a pool.
In any year, only a few suffer a big loss, like a house fire or serious car crash, and the pool pays.
Insurers use statistics to set premiums and add costs and profit, so on average customers pay in more than they get back.
That's fine: you're buying protection, not an investment.
The golden rule is to insure what you can't afford to lose: your house, a year of income, or liability for injuring someone.
Extended warranties and insurance on cheap items such as phones are often poor value, because Australian Consumer Law already gives you a repair, replacement or refund for major faults.
An emergency fund lets you 'self-insure' small losses and choose higher excesses.
Cover for you.
Medicare gives free public-patient treatment in public hospitals.
Private hospital cover lets you choose your doctor, and extras cover pays towards dental and physio.
Since 2019, hospital policies are grouped as Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic.

The Medicare Levy Surcharge taxes higher earners without appropriate hospital cover, and Lifetime Health Cover adds 2% to premiums for each year over 30 before you first join, up to 70%, removed after ten continuous years.
Your income is often your biggest asset.
Income protection commonly pays up to around 70% of income if illness or injury stops you working.
Life cover pays your beneficiaries a lump sum; total and permanent disability, TPD, cover pays if you can never work again; trauma cover pays on diagnosis of serious illness.
Super funds often provide some by default, but premiums reduce your balance.
Cover for your things.
Home building insurance covers the structure; contents covers your belongings, and renters usually need only contents.
Check whether flood, storm and bushfire are covered, as these matter hugely in Australia.
For cars, Compulsory Third Party, CTP, insurance, generally tied to your registration, covers injuries you cause to other people, but not damage to cars or property.
Third-party property cover pays for damage you do to other people's cars and property.
Adding fire and theft covers your own car for those events, and comprehensive cover also pays for damage to your own car.
Crashing into a luxury car without property cover can be very costly.
Excess and premium.
The excess is the amount you pay out of your own pocket when you make a claim.
If your car repair costs $4,000 and your excess is $800, the insurer pays $3,200.
Choosing a higher excess usually lowers your premium, which can make sense if you have savings to cover it and rarely claim.
Some policies have different excesses for different situations, such as young or unlisted drivers.
Premiums also depend on your address, claims history and what's being insured.
Don't just auto-renew.
Premiums often rise each year, so compare at renewal and ask your current insurer for a better price.
Fine print and gaps.
Every policy has a Product Disclosure Statement, PDS, and home insurance also has a shorter Key Facts Sheet.
A few minutes on the right sections can save thousands.
Check exclusions, limits such as caps on jewellery or laptops, and definitions like 'flood'.
Answer questions honestly, because misleading information can void a claim.
If the insurer's complaints process fails, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, AFCA, offers a free dispute service.
Being underinsured means your cover can't replace what you lose.
After bushfires and floods, many households found their sum insured couldn't cover a rebuild, as costs had risen or demolition and code upgrades weren't counted.
Use a building cost calculator, tally contents room by room, and review cover yearly.
This is general information only; talk to a licensed adviser.
The key idea: Insurance pools many people's premiums to pay large losses, so insure what you couldn't afford to lose and self-insure the rest.
Part four. Income protection: insuring your pay.
Your ability to earn may be worth more than your house or car, yet many people insure those and not their income.
Here is how income protection works, and the questions to ask before you buy or keep it.
Insuring your pay.
Ask people for their most valuable asset and they name their home or car.
But for a working adult, the pay they expect to earn over coming decades is often worth far more.
Illness or injury that stops you working for months can drain savings fast while bills keep arriving.
Income protection pays a regular monthly benefit while you can't work because of a covered illness or injury.
It replaces only part of your income, commonly up to around 70 percent in many current policies, which keeps an incentive to return to work.
It differs from life insurance, which pays on death, and total and permanent disability cover, which pays a lump sum.
Definitions of being unable to work vary, so read the product disclosure statement.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Waiting and benefit periods.
Two choices shape both the cost and usefulness of a policy.
The waiting period is how long you must be unable to work before benefits start, often 30, 60 or 90 days, or longer.
A longer wait usually means a cheaper premium, which can suit you if you have sick leave or an emergency fund to bridge the gap.
The benefit period is how long payments can continue once they start, such as two years, five years or until a set age.
Longer periods cost more but protect against long-term illness, which does the most financial damage.
Think about how long your savings and leave could realistically carry you, then compare combinations.
Inside or outside super.
Many people already have income protection through their super fund without realising it.
Check your fund's website or annual statement.
Cover inside super is paid from your super balance, which spares your weekly budget but reduces your retirement savings.
It often has shorter benefit periods and stricter definitions than standalone policies.
Default cover can be switched off if your account has been inactive for a period, or for some younger members and low balances, unless you opt in.
A standalone policy, bought directly or through an adviser, can usually be tailored more closely.
You can hold both, but benefits may be offset so you can't claim more than the limits allow.
Compare before you add or cancel anything.
Tax and premiums.
The tax treatment surprises some people.
If you pay premiums for income protection held outside super, the ATO generally lets you claim them as a deduction, because the policy replaces taxable income.
The flip side is that benefit payments are generally taxable income too.
Premiums paid from within super aren't claimed in your personal return.
If a policy bundles income protection with other cover, such as life insurance, only the income protection part is usually deductible, and your insurer should show the split.
Premiums can be stepped, rising with age, or level, starting higher but rising more slowly.
Both generally increase over time.
Check the ATO website for the rules that apply to you.
Disclosure and other safety nets.
When applying, you'll be asked about your health, job, income and lifestyle.
Answer fully and honestly.
Under Australian law you must take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation, and inaccurate answers can let the insurer reduce a payout, refuse a claim or cancel the policy.
Get quotes from more than one insurer or speak to a licensed adviser, and compare disability definitions, benefit amounts, waiting and benefit periods and exclusions, not just price.
Income protection is one layer.
Paid personal leave covers short absences.
Workers compensation may cover work-related injury or illness.
Services Australia income support is means-tested and usually far below a working wage.
Knowing where these end helps you choose how much private cover makes sense.
The key idea: Income protection replaces part of your income, typically a monthly benefit of up to about 70 percent, if illness or injury stops you working.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the Super Guarantee require employers to do?
Answer. Add a share of your pay to super on top of wages.
Question two. What does 'stapling' mean in Australian super?
Answer. Your fund usually follows you to a new job.
Question three. What is the golden rule for deciding what to insure?
Answer. Insure losses you couldn't afford to cover yourself.
Question four. How does income protection differ from life insurance?
Answer. It replaces part of your pay when you can't work.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
